papers.abstract: Long-context models repeatedly solve closely related retrieval problems. Attention or global retrieval can retain large stores, but each forward pass again searches for what matters. Recurrent compression avoids this search only by deciding earlier what information to preserve. Neither mechanism directly exploits that useful memories at neighbouring retrieval steps may substantially overlap. We propose an alternative in which retrieval is a persistent local traversal through an address space. We separate a memory's content from its address. Utility is defined by the information revealed by retrieving the content, while geometry determines only how cheaply that information can be reached. This leads to a cost-regularised indexing objective that preserves information value inside local neighbourhoods while charging for every memory made locally accessible. Its marginal-value form gives both attractive and exclusion pressures. Thus, complementary memories should be co-retrievable when the additional value exceeds retrieval cost, whereas redundant memories should not occupy the same retrieval set solely because they are individually useful. As a proof of principle, we test only the simplest fixed-geometry instance on MiniGrid Memory. A persistent local traversal head reaches $0.95$ mean return after $0.59$M training steps with a five-token context, compared with $0.94$M for Gaussian absolute addressing and more than $2$M for categorical absolute addressing. The experiment does not test learned geometry or repeated retrieval. Instead, it motivates the hypothesis that stateful retrieval may be easier to learn than stateless. To test the full proposed method further experimentation is necessary.
authors: Daniel Strau{\ss}, Zhenshan Bing, Alois Knoll
bullets: Motivation: Global retrieval repeatedly searches large stores, while recurrent compression risks discarding information too early.
Method: Separate memory content from address and optimize local neighborhoods using retrieval information value minus accessibility cost.
Key principle: Complementary memories should be co-retrievable when their added value exceeds cost; redundant memories should be excluded despite individual usefulness.
Proof of principle: On MiniGrid Memory, fixed-geometry traversal reached 0.95 mean return after 0.59M steps, versus 0.94M for Gaussian absolute addressing and over 2M for categorical addressing.
Scope: The experiment does not evaluate learned geometry or repeated retrieval, so the full method remains unvalidated.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes value-indexed memory for stateful long-context agents, tested on MiniGrid Memory; directly relevant to embodied memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Retrieval as Traversal: Value-Indexed Memory for Stateful Long-Context Agents
papers.tldr: A value-indexed, persistent local traversal mechanism aims to make stateful retrieval easier by grouping complementary memories while avoiding redundant co-retrieval.

papers.abstract: Modern LLMs strain device memory through large model weights and attention states, particularly in resource-constrained scenarios. Existing systems separately provision memory for model weights and attention states, imposing fixed fixed boundaries that cannot adapt to the changing memory demands of workloads. Under heavy workloads, insufficient state capacity limits request concurrency and reduces throughput; under light workloads, idle memory in one region cannot be reallocated to another, wasting device memory. Meanwhile, modern LLM architectures introduce heterogeneous tensors with diverse layouts and lifetimes, further complicating memory management. These problems motivate unified memory management for heterogeneous tensors. However, a shared pool alone does not make memory directly reusable across tensors with different allocation granularities and execution layouts. This paper presents Rimuru, a modern LLM serving system that unifies memory management through elastic expert offloading. Rimuru establishes a shared page pool to enables elastic memory sharing across heterogeneous tensors. To accommodate different allocation granularities, Rimuru introduces memory views that allow each tensor type to interpret the shared memory space using its own page size and page table. Furthermore, Rimuru combines huge-page alignment with a multi-level page allocator that splits and merges pages, enabling cross-type capacity reuse. A page-table-aware fused MoE kernel directly accesses non-contiguous expert weights, avoiding copy overhead. Building on these mechanisms, Rimuru employs a workload-aware adjuster that dynamically reallocates pages across tensor types according to runtime demands. Implemented on top of vLLM, Rimuru remains compatible with modern LLMs. Evaluations show that Rimuru achieves up to 19.03x baseline throughput and reduces TTFT by 98.1% on average.
bullets: Fixed partitions for model weights and attention states waste memory and limit concurrency under changing workloads.
Rimuru uses a shared page pool with tensor-specific memory views and page tables to support different layouts and allocation granularities.
A multi-level allocator enables page splitting, merging, and cross-tensor capacity reuse, while a fused MoE kernel accesses non-contiguous expert weights without copying.
A workload-aware adjuster reallocates pages at runtime based on demand and is implemented in vLLM.
The system reports up to 19.03× baseline throughput and an average 98.1% reduction in time to first token (TTFT).

papers.abstract: Robotic navigation typically assumes a collision-free route to the goal exists; in cluttered environments with movable obstacles, however, reaching the goal may require physical interaction. Classical solutions encode these behaviors through geometric rules and task-specific logic, while learning-based approaches often constrain the decision space to low-dimensional motion commands or predefined action sets. We instead consider a broader decision space, jointly selecting the skill, relevant object, and geometric target. Our language-conditioned task planner, fine-tuned with LoRA on synthetic data, maps natural-language tasks and a structured scene representation to variable-length sequences of parameterized actions, executed by low-level reinforcement-learning policies. The planner learns the geometric relations underlying interactive navigation and outperforms a classical planner and a prompted frontier model on interactive navigation tasks. Comparisons with models trained from scratch indicate that composition does not require pretraining when the representation is structured, whereas pretraining yields more reliable geometric targets. At the low level, we introduce an end-to-end whole-body planar pushing policy that achieves a 93.3% success rate in simulation, versus 83.5% for a hierarchical baseline, while reducing completion time by more than 60%. On hardware, the hierarchy yields the correct skill composition in 44/45 trials and end-to-end success in 34/45. Project website: https://anonymousprojects-dev.github.io/LLM-guided-LocoManipulation-Quadrupeds/
bullets: Addresses navigation tasks where movable obstacles require physical interaction rather than collision-free motion alone.
Jointly selects the skill, relevant object, and geometric target, producing variable-length parameterized action sequences from language and structured scene representations.
Uses a LoRA-fine-tuned language-conditioned planner with low-level reinforcement-learning policies, including an end-to-end whole-body planar pushing policy.
The pushing policy achieves 93.3% simulation success versus 83.5% for a hierarchical baseline and reduces completion time by over 60%.
On hardware, the planner composes the correct skills in 44/45 trials, with end-to-end success in 34/45.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models excel at instruction following, yet most remain feed-forward: they condition actions only on the current observation and discard both long-horizon temporal context and the hierarchical structure of VLM representations. We present PRIME W0, a hierarchical conditional flow-matching framework that closes this gap through three synergistic designs: (1)per-layer KV injection from a pretrained VLM into an Adaptive MoE action expert; (2)dynamics-aware conditioning via asynchronous world-model subgoal-image prediction and a DINOv2 historical-frame semantic bridge; and (3)Action Dynamic Manifold (ADM) flow matching with covariance-structured noise that respects robot kinematic coupling. PRIME W0 is trained in four stages---VLM pre-training, DAT/NTP visuomotor pre-training, DiT flow-matching decoder assembly with WM injection, and end-to-end SFT---and achieves state-of-the-art results on LIBERO and real-robot benchmarks, with systematic ablations validating each architectural component.
bullets: Addresses the limitations of feed-forward VLA models, which ignore long-horizon context and hierarchical visual-language representations.
Injects pretrained VLM key-value features into an adaptive mixture-of-experts action module.
Uses asynchronous world-model subgoal-image prediction and DINOv2 historical-frame features for dynamics-aware temporal conditioning.
Applies covariance-structured flow matching on an Action Dynamic Manifold to model coupled robot actions.
Reports state-of-the-art performance on LIBERO and real-robot benchmarks, with ablations supporting the proposed components.

figures.caption: Figure 1: PRIME W0 architecture.

Figure 2: Four-stage training pipeline. (1) VLM Pretrain: the vision–language backbone is trained on general multimodal supervision (e.g. captioning / VQA). (2) NTP / task-specific pre-training: with DAT action tokens, the VLM learns visuomotor next-token prediction over instruction–observation–action sequences. (3) DiT Pretrain: the VLM is frozen while the MoT / Adaptive MoE flow-matching action expert is trained with world-model conditioning to denoise continuous actions (and associated state tokens). (4) SFT: both the VLM and the action expert are jointly fine-tuned end-to-end, optionally with action-prefix tokens that shorten the denoising trajectory at inference. Flame / snowflake icons indicate trainable vs. frozen modules.

Figure 5: Scaling with world-model capacity. LIBERO-Long success scales monotonically with WM size; the largest gain is between 5M and 50M parameters (+5.9%). Better subgoal-image prediction directly benefits the asynchronous WM→VLM→ADM pipeline.

Figure 3: Training data mixture. Robot demonstration data used by PRIME W0 totals approximately 10,000 hours, comprising Teleop (60%, ∼6,000 h; laboratory setups, data-collection factories, and public datasets), UMI (30%, ∼3,000 h; portable UMI fisheye egocentric collection), and Simulation (10%, ∼1,000 h; reconstructed scenes with procedural objects and physics randomisation).

Figure 4: ADM cross-attention to WM subgoal-image tokens across manipulation phases. Attention to WMpredicted subgoal tokens peaks at contact-establishment and placement phases, confirming that forward scene predictions actively condition manifold-constrained action generation during critical moments.

Table 4: Component ablation. Each row adds one module on top of the previous variant. Metrics: LIBERO-Long success (%) and real-robot average success (%).

papers.selection_reason: Hierarchical VLA with world-model subgoal prediction for manipulation; fits embodied AI, world models, and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: PRIME W0: Physical Priors from World Models for Embodied Manipulation
papers.tldr: PRIME W0 enhances vision-language-action models for embodied manipulation by combining hierarchical VLM features, world-model dynamics, temporal context, and kinematics-aware action generation.

papers.abstract: We study domain generalization for LIDAR semantic segmentation. Deep neural networks achieve strong performance on 3D point clouds, yet real-world LIDAR exhibits sensor-specific sampling patterns that hinder transfer across datasets. In many applications, performance on completely unseen sensors is crucial. A model should preferably work on a new setup without prior access to its data or labels. To this end, we introduce a source-only training scheme that adds an occupancy prediction auxiliary objective. We aggregate source-domain scans into a simple world model and use it as the supervision signal, replacing single-scan standard segmentation training. A key property of our approach is that it does not alter the input scan. During training and testing the network consumes the same single-frame LIDAR input, only the supervision signal is enriched via the occupancy objective. At deployment, there is no runtime overhead as the auxiliary head can be dropped for pure segmentation, or kept to obtain scene completion alongside semantic segmentation. In an experimental evaluation across distinct LIDAR datasets, we demonstrate that a model's generalization to new domains can be significantly affected by how it is supervised. In certain setups, performance on unseen domains improves without any explicit domain adaptation (no target scans, no target labels, no sensor priors) and without prediction refinement. At the same time, our method maintains competitive source-domain segmentation performance and incurs no additional inference cost.
bullets: Targets sensor-specific sampling differences that hinder cross-dataset LiDAR segmentation.
Aggregates source scans into a world model and uses occupancy prediction as an auxiliary training objective.
The network still processes a single-frame scan; only the supervision is enriched.
Unseen-domain performance improves in some settings without domain adaptation, target scans, labels, sensor priors, or prediction refinement.
Source-domain performance remains competitive, with no runtime overhead; the auxiliary head can optionally provide scene completion.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Proposed method: We add an occupancy prediction task based on accumulated LiDAR points while training on the source domain to improve model generalization (orange blocks). When this task is removed at test time, a vanilla semantic segmentation model remains. Even during domain generalization training, the input to the model is unchanged. Data for the occupancy prediction is generated automatically on the source domain.

Fig. 3: Dataset characteristics. Accumulated world-frame ground truth is semantically color-coded by the 10-A label set. Rows illustrate differing LIDAR configurations across datasets. KITTI uses a single 64-beam LIDAR, yielding up to 115k points within 100 ms. nuScenes fuses the five most recent 32-beam scans over 250 ms. Waymo employs multiple LIDARs to reduce blind spots.

Fig. 4: Qualitative Results: Examples of cross-sensor domain generalization with two evaluation examples from the nuScenes and two from the Waymo dataset (one per row). Each row displays, from left to right: ground truth reference, segmentation result trained on (a) nuScenes accumulated points, (b) nuScenes segmentation, (c) Waymo accumulated points, (d) Waymo segmentation. For clarity, all unlabeled points (gray) are shown as unlabeled in the prediction columns. A gray border highlights source-domain evaluation; green background highlights improvements on the unseen target domain. Training on accumulated multi-scan points in the source domain yields a noticeably more robust network. Ground segmentation issues due to scan patterns are effectively reduced and object boundaries are more consistent. Importantly, no visible regression is observed on the source domain when using accumulated points compared to standard segmentation.

Fig. 1: Sensor-to-sensor Domain Generalization with richer supervision: Comparing two training signals on the source domain (nuScenes) and their effect on the target domain (Waymo) segmentation task (blue: car, green: vegetation, magenta: ground). The left column uses standard per-scan semantic segmentation, the right column uses accumulated multi-scan points as supervision signal. When evaluated on an unseen target domain sensor (bottom row), the accumulated points training is robust against sensor ground patterns and yields correct predictions with consistent boundaries.

papers.title: Robust LIDAR Sensor-to-Sensor Domain Generalization via Accumulated-Point Scene Completion

papers.abstract: Human cognition flexibly draws on a shared perceptual foundation to understand environments, attend to referenced entities, reason about spatial relationships, and act. Endowing aerial robots with an analogous functional organization remains challenging, as existing systems are often specialized for individual capabilities, dependent on offboard computation, or unable to sustain closed-loop operation on resource-constrained platforms. We present OpenFlyV2, a unified onboard vision-language-action architecture that uses a shared vision-language representation to support semantic understanding, language-grounded perception, spatial reasoning, and continuous aerial control within a single model. A compact action expert converts the shared multimodal context into short-horizon flight waypoints, while motion-aware temporal memory and action priors reduce the computational cost of closed-loop execution. We construct \dataset{}, a simulation-based dataset comprising approximately 70,000 navigation trajectories and 60,000 vision-language instruction--response pairs. OpenFlyV2 generates action chunks, each comprising 12 waypoints, entirely onboard at 10 Hz using an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX. It transfers zero-shot from simulation to physical quadrotor flight, achieving a 48\% navigation success rate across four real-world environments without real-world aerial training data. Extensive results demonstrate that broad vision-language competence and continuous closed-loop flight can coexist within a single model on a resource-constrained aerial platform. Code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/Ideal-ljl/AeroBrain.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of unifying aerial perception, language grounding, reasoning, and control without offboard computation.
Uses a shared vision-language representation, a compact waypoint-generating action expert, temporal memory, and action priors.
Trains on approximately 70,000 simulated navigation trajectories and 60,000 vision-language instruction–response pairs.
Runs onboard at 10 Hz on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX, producing 12-waypoint action chunks.
Transfers zero-shot to physical flight, achieving a 48% navigation success rate across four real-world environments without real-world aerial training data.

figures.caption: Figure 6. Architecture of OpenFlyV2. (A) A shared vision-language backbone encodes the current image, instruction, and memory tokens to condition action generation. (B) Motion-Adaptive Memory (MAM) compresses historical action segments and their visual anchors into compact event-level tokens. (C) The Motion-Structured Prior (MSP) selects and adjusts a data-derived motion prototype to construct the action source distribution. The action expert transforms a sample from this distribution into the final action chunk through conditional flow matching.

Figure 4. Quantitative evaluation of aerial understanding and navigation. (A) Comparison with general-purpose vision-language models on color recognition, description generation, visual grounding, distance estimation, and spatial relationship reasoning. Visual grounding is reported as accuracy at an IoU threshold of 0.5 (Acc@0.5), and distance estimation is shown as relative error. (B) Navigation performance in seen and unseen simulated environments, measured by success rate (SR), oracle success rate (OSR), success weighted by path length (SPL), and navigation error (NE). The navigation baselines were trained on our aerial navigation dataset and evaluated on the same 800 seen and 300 unseen episodes as OpenFlyV2. Success requires an explicit stop within 25 m of the goal. Blue and orange bars in (B) indicate seen and unseen environments, respectively. Arrows indicate the direction of better performance.

Figure 2. Shared environments and data composition of OpenFlyV2-130K. (A) Thirteen environments supporting both navigation and VQA: four AirSim environments, two Unreal Engine city environments, and seven 3DGS reconstructions of real campuses and post-disaster ruins. (B) Distribution of 72,352 navigation trajectories across the environments. (C) Distribution of 60,006 VQA pairs across color recognition, object description, distance estimation, spatial relationship reasoning, and visual grounding.

Figure 3. Aerial vision-language understanding and spatial reasoning with OpenFlyV2. (A) Distance estimation for the building marked in green: 179 m compared with a reference distance of approximately 180 m. (B) Description of the building within the yellow box. (C) Relative-distance reasoning identifies the red-box building as closer to the camera than the blue-box building. (D) Localization of a language-described target. The predicted bounding box (dashed orange) and reference box (solid cyan) have an intersection over union (IoU) of 0.753.
Figure 5. Onboard aerial vision-language navigation. Three physical flight trials performed by OpenFlyV2 on a DJI M30T, with all navigation inference executed on an onboard NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX.

The Steps column reports the number of flow-integration (denoising) steps; SR, OSR, and SPL are percentages, and NE is in meters. papers.title: OpenFlyV2: An onboard vision-language-action model for aerial perception and navigation
papers.tldr: OpenFlyV2 is an onboard vision-language-action model that combines semantic understanding, spatial reasoning, and closed-loop aerial control on a resource-constrained drone.

papers.abstract: Video captioning models are increasingly evaluated with metrics designed for single-sentence image captions. We test whether those metrics recover human judgement on dense, multi-window video description, and find that they do not. Six frontier models captioned 196 short clips. Trained annotators post-edited every caption against a failure taxonomy fixed before annotation, once as a whole-clip overview and once window by window, and a quality-control reviewer checked each annotation, yielding 1,144 overview verdicts and 4,672 window verdicts. Reference-overlap metrics do not separate the captions reviewers accepted from those they rejected: BLEU-4 reaches an AUC of 0.510 and a CIDEr-style tf-idf cosine 0.528, and restricting references to reviewer corrections leaves BLEU-4 at 0.479 (95% CI 0.431-0.529), indistinguishable from chance. Review granularity changes what is detected. The same annotators record camera and shot errors on 2.7% of captions when reading the overview and on 12.8% when reading window by window, a 4.7x gap that holds across every robustness check we ran, on the mode most likely to need a near-total rewrite. Correct-overview rates span 54.1-72.7%, but only 4 of 15 pairwise gaps survive Bonferroni correction (5 after adjusting for reviewer and clip effects), and accuracy and derived severity order the models differently. Models with statistically indistinguishable accuracy have sharply different failure profiles, which no single scalar shows. We argue that caption evaluation should record what was wrong rather than only how often, and we report the taxonomy, the per-model profiles, the corpus properties that predict difficulty, and the code that regenerates every number in the paper.
bullets: Six models captioned 196 short clips, with human corrections assessed for whole-clip overviews and window-by-window descriptions.
BLEU-4 and CIDEr-style scores were essentially chance-level at distinguishing accepted from rejected captions.
Window-by-window review detected camera and shot errors 4.7× more often than overview review.
Models with similar overall accuracy showed sharply different failure types, and accuracy and severity ranked models differently.
The study advocates reporting failure taxonomies and per-model error profiles instead of relying on a single scalar score.

papers.selection_reason: Video caption evaluation with human correction taxonomy; fits video-language understanding.
papers.title: Similar Scores, Opposite Failures: Human Correction as an Instrument for Video Caption Evaluation

papers.abstract: A key challenge of RAG systems is retrieving information from enterprise documents created by multiple teams over time, where it is not possible to enrich the information using the latest information and metadata available outside the scope of organizational documentation responsibility. We investigated whether using a knowledge graph to store metadata and frequently changing information would improve upon knowledge retrieval over similarity search over embeddings. To perform the experiment, we created a snapshot of the SEC EDGAR dataset for a quarter, comprising 167,050 filings from 10,511 companies and 508,714 embedded chunks of risk-factor text. To simulate the enrichment, we created a knowledge graph of 430,257 nodes and 561,144 edges carrying an accession number on every edge. To evaluate the gain obtained via a graph-based design, we evaluated three architectures: text-to-SQL over typed columns, dense-vector RAG with HNSW cosine search, and a two-stage GraphRAG design. All architectures share the same model and temperature to allow comparison. Results are scored programmatically by an LLM as judge over 20 questions divided across four categories, each question asked three times. GraphRAG solved 16 of 20 questions on all three attempts, compared to 10 for text-to-SQL and 3 for vector RAG. GraphRAG lost on structured aggregation queries. Vector RAG lost the single-document category it was expected to win, passing 3 of 15 where GraphRAG passed 15 of 15, because company attribution is not recoverable from cosine similarity at this scale. All six confident falsehoods in the benchmark were text-to-SQL conflating distinct people who share a surname, the failure that resolving identity to an identifier before reading any text prevents structurally; GraphRAG made none. We claim no advantage beyond this corpus, this model and this question set.
bullets: Enterprise documents can lack current external metadata and reliable organizational context.
The study compares text-to-SQL, HNSW dense-vector RAG, and two-stage GraphRAG using a knowledge graph of changing metadata and identifiers.
GraphRAG answered all three repetitions of 16/20 questions, versus 10/20 for text-to-SQL and 3/20 for vector RAG.
GraphRAG performed especially well on company attribution and single-document questions, and avoided the benchmark’s identity-related falsehoods.
The authors limit their claim to the tested corpus, model, and question set; GraphRAG underperformed on structured aggregation queries.

figures.caption: Figure 4: The three retrieval arms over shared stores. Text-to-SQL and GraphRAG use two LLM calls each; vector RAG uses one and has no query language to repair. In GraphRAG only the first hop is LLM-authored: entity expansion is deterministic and system-authored, which is what prevents one entity’s fan-out from consuming the row budget and the model then reporting that the other entities do not exist.

Figure 6: The economics. (a) Text-to-SQL’s T3 mean is the SQL and not the model: the generated queries join three tables without narrowing first. (b) GraphRAG’s accuracy is bought: it has the highest token cost per passing attempt of the three, the exact figures being in Table 3.

Figure 1: The three facts a multi-hop question needs live in three different containers. Item 1A is narrative prose and is the only section embedded; EX-21 is a structured list attached to the same filing; insider roles are in a separate filing type entirely. Every projected edge carries the accession number of the filing that asserts it.

Figure 2: Corpus shape. (a) EX-21 disclosure is extremely skewed — 275 filers list one subsidiary, 62 list more than 500 — so any generated LIMIT over a join to this table starves whole entities unless rows are balanced per entity first. (b) The small 2025-08 bucket is spillover, since a monthly feed contains filings dated at the end of the preceding month.

Figure 5: Results. The composition in (b) matters as much as the rate in (a): vector RAG’s 45 refusals are a benign failure, text-to-SQL’s 16 uncited answers are right but unverifiable, and GraphRAG was never uncited because the traversal returns accession numbers before any text is read.

Figure 3: Ingestion wall-clock, about 252 minutes total. Document fetch and embedding are roughly 82% of it. The fetch component is bounded externally by EDGAR’s ten-requests-per-second fair-access policy and cannot be parallelized away.
Figure 7: Repair frequency by category. GraphRAG required a repair on all fifteen T4 attempts, which is the entity-resolution category it lost.

Table 7: Cross-model probe on the featured multi-hop question with the GraphRAG pipeline held constant. One question and one attempt per model, so this is a probe rather than a measurement; it supports only the negative conclusion that a single-model benchmark bounds what can be claimed.

Table 9: The twenty benchmark questions. T1 single-document semantic, T2 structured aggregation, T3 multi-hop relational plus text, T4 cross-document entity resolution.
Table 8: Monthly infrastructure cost, on-demand pricing in ap-south-1. The embedding pass used a temporarily resized 16-vCPU host at 97 chunks/s; the instance was scaled back afterwards.

Table 1: The loaded corpus. Twelve monthly EDGAR feeds, 2025-09 through 2026-08. Node and edge counts are live counts from the graph; the per-type edge breakdown in Section 3 sums exactly to the total shown here.

Table 2: Narrative sections extracted per 10-K Item. Only Item 1A (bold) is embedded, giving 508,714 chunks. Its mean length exceeds the encoder’s 256-word-piece window by roughly two orders of magnitude, which is why chunking is forced rather than optional.

Table 4: Per-category results. Q = questions solved on all three attempts (of 5); A = attempts passed (of 15). Two of the four categories were pre-registered as ones the graph should lose. It lost T2 as expected and T4 against expectation.

papers.selection_reason: Knowledge-graph-backed retrieval acts as persistent external memory for LLMs, fitting the LLM memory subtopic.
papers.title: Beyond Similarity Search: Knowledge Graph Metadata Enrichment for Enterprise Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.tldr: A two-stage GraphRAG design improved enterprise retrieval over dense-vector RAG and text-to-SQL in a controlled SEC filing benchmark, while remaining weaker on structured aggregation queries.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing editable and compositional 3D scenes from a real image requires jointly reasoning about geometry, object structure, and spatial relationships. We introduce SceneEvolve, a framework that represents 3D scenes as executable code and improves reconstruction by evolving the harness around a small open-source agent. SceneEvolve combines SceneAct, a compositional semantic action interface built on parameterized primitives, hierarchical composition, and semantic spatial relations, with SceneHarness-RSI, which leverages a stronger teacher agent to iteratively evolve the harness using feedback from development-set reconstructions. Throughout harness evolution, the model parameters, action semantics, and execution backend remain fixed. The resulting harness provides a reusable reconstruction procedure that enables the small open-source model to reconstruct unseen scenes without parameter updates or teacher assistance. Across two in-domain datasets and one out-of-domain dataset, SceneEvolve with the comparatively compact Qwen3.8-27B model improves all four evaluated reconstruction metrics while reducing mean inference time by 47.0% relative to the base model. More notably, despite relying on a substantially smaller model, SceneEvolve achieves 32.3% higher reconstruction quality than the large proprietary GPT-5.6-Sol model, while reducing mean equivalent deployment cost by 59.8%. Furthermore, the harness evolved using Qwen3.8-27B also generalizes to Kimi-K3, achieving comparable reconstruction performance to GPT-6-Astra. The project page is https://haoyu-agent.github.io/SceneEvolve.
bullets: Represents scenes as executable code and uses compositional actions, parameterized primitives, hierarchical structure, and semantic spatial relations.
A stronger teacher iteratively evolves the reconstruction harness from development-set feedback while keeping model parameters, action semantics, and execution fixed.
The resulting procedure enables small models to reconstruct unseen scenes without further parameter updates or teacher assistance.
Across three datasets, the approach improved all four evaluated metrics and reduced mean inference time by 47.0% versus the base model.
It reportedly outperformed larger proprietary models in reconstruction quality and deployment cost, and transferred effectively to another model family.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Illustration of SCENEEVOLVE for compositional image-to-3D reconstruction. The framework combines two components: (1) SCENEACT translates scene intent into executable Blender operations through parameterized primitives, hierarchical composition, and semantic spatial relations. (2) SCENEHARNESS-RSI couples an outer loop for teacher-guided harness evolution with an inner loop for candidate evaluation by a frozen student, retaining revisions that improve performance. The optimized harness is deployed on unseen scenes without parameter updates.

Figure 4: Comparison of reconstruction quality against inference time and equivalent deployment cost across model configurations. The high, medium and low settings denote reasoning modes from deeper to shallower inference. DINOv2-S ↑, inference time ↓, and equivalent deployment cost ↓ are reported averaged over three datasets.

Figure 6: Qualitative comparisons of indoor scene reconstruction with GPT-6-Astra, GPT-5.6-Sol, Qwen3.8-27B and Kimi-K3 on Scannet, CA-1M and ARKitScenes datasets. SCENEEVOLVE reconstructs editable 3D scenes that capture object geometry, relative proportions, and spatial relationships in the reference images, demonstrating improved structural fidelity.

Figure 5: Comparison of SCENEEVOLVE with Qwen3.8-27B at xhigh, GPT-5.6-Sol at none, and GPT-6-Astra at none on two in-domain datasets ScanNet and CA-1M and the out-of-domain dataset ARKitScenes. The DINOv2 similarity, inference time, and deployment cost are reported for each.
Figure 3: Comparison of SCENEEVOLVE with Qwen3.8-27B at xhigh, GPT-5.6-Sol at none, and GPT-6-Astra at none. The average DINOv2-S ↑, inference time ↓, and equivalent cost ↓ are reported.

Table 1: Performance comparison across different models on ScanNet and CA-1M (in-domain) and ARKitScenes (out-of-domain). We report PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and DINOv2 similarity. GPT-6Astra serves as the reference. The best and second results are highlighted in bold and underlined.
Table 2: Component-ablation on Qwen3.8-27B, averaged across the three datasets. PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, DINOv2 similarity, inference time, and equivalent cost are averaged across the three datasets.

papers.selection_reason: Compositional 3D reconstruction from images via evolved agent harness; directly fits 3D vision perception/generation.
papers.title: Learning to Code the World: Harness Evolution for Compositional 3D Reconstruction
papers.tldr: SceneEvolve improves editable, compositional 3D reconstruction by evolving a reusable code-based harness around a small open-source agent, without updating the model itself.

papers.abstract: Multimodal learning often suffers from modality imbalance, where the joint optimization process is dominated by a single modality. Existing methods typically estimate modality imbalance from score disparities derived from prediction uncertainty or optimization statistics. However, due to distinct prediction uncertainty and learning dynamics across modalities, direct comparison of such scores may misinterpret intrinsic modality differences as progress gaps, leading to biased imbalance estimation. In this paper, we propose Function-Space Guided Multimodal Optimization (FGMO), which leverages a function-space progress signal to assess modality-wise optimization progress and coordinate optimization across modalities to alleviate modality imbalance. Specifically, we introduce Functional Progress Estimation (FPE) to measure each modality's update-induced function-space response and calibrate it against a loss-aligned unimodal reference, producing a comparable progress signal. Based on this signal, Functional Response Control (FRC) redistributes modality-level function-space budgets and realizes the target responses through tensor-wise learning-rate adjustment. Theoretical analysis establishes a one-step target-contraction property of FRC under bounded controller-state mismatch, and extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of FGMO across multiple multimodal benchmarks.
bullets: Addresses modality imbalance caused by optimization being dominated by one modality.
Uses Functional Progress Estimation to measure update-induced function changes relative to a loss-aligned unimodal reference.
Applies Functional Response Control to redistribute modality-level function-space budgets through tensor-wise learning-rate adjustment.
Provides a theoretical one-step target-contraction guarantee under bounded controller-state mismatch.
Experiments across multiple multimodal benchmarks demonstrate FGMO’s effectiveness.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The overall framework of Function-Space Guided Multimodal Optimization (FGMO). FPE estimates Relative Functional Progress (RFP) from update-induced function-space responses and loss-aligned unimodal references, while FRC uses RFP feedback to perform modality-level response allocation and tensor-wise learning-rate adjustment.

Figure 5: (a) Beneficial Rates of different modality signals under controlled interventions. (b) Training-time comparison with representative multimodal learning methods. (c) Tensor-wise learning-rate allocation across the audio and video branches, where each cell reports the geometricmean learning-rate multiplier.

Figure 4: Sensitivity analysis of the controller gain λ on the Sarcasm and CREMA-D datasets. (a) and (b) Evolution of the absolute log RFP ratio | log Qt| under different controller gains on Sarcasm and CREMA-D, respectively. (c) Impact of λ on the multimodal classification accuracy. The dashed line (λ = 2) denotes the boundary of the ideal target-contraction range.

Table 1: Comparison with SOTA multimodal learning methods. The best results are highlighted in bold. The underline denotes the second-best performance. Gray-shaded results indicate that multimodal performance is lower than that of the best unimodal approach.

papers.selection_reason: Function-space method to balance multimodal optimization; transferable to multimodal foundation model training.
papers.title: Balancing Multimodal Learning via Functional Progress
papers.tldr: FGMO balances multimodal optimization by comparing modality progress in function space and adjusting learning rates to coordinate their contributions.

papers.abstract: Deep learning has shown remarkable success in the data-driven modeling of dynamical systems. Much of its success is attributed not to the flexibility of neural networks but to inductive biases based on physical prior knowledge, such as energy conservation and symplecticity. However, existing methods do not fully exploit the fact that real-world physical systems are interconnections of components. Some methods require the interconnection to be known a priori, while others assume the system to be reducible to an ordinary differential equation (ODE) and learn only the reduced ODE, discarding the algebraic constraints imposed by the interconnection. Here, we propose Dirac-interconnected neural elements (DINEs), a neural network model that represents a physical system as a differential-algebraic equation (DAE), whose algebraic constraints are given by a Dirac structure in kernel representation. With DINEs, we simultaneously identify from data the interconnection among the components as a Dirac structure and learn the characteristics of the components as neural networks. This allows us to keep the learned subsystems in unreduced form and isolate or compose them to make a new system without retraining. Moreover, DINEs can handle partially observable systems. Experimental results demonstrate these capabilities on physical systems beyond the reach of existing methods.
bullets: Targets a limitation of existing physics-informed models: known interconnections or ODE reduction can discard algebraic constraints.
Represents physical systems as differential-algebraic equations with Dirac structures in kernel form.
Jointly identifies subsystem interconnections and learns subsystem characteristics with neural networks.
Supports partially observable systems and enables subsystem isolation or recombination without retraining.
Experiments demonstrate these capabilities on physical systems beyond the reach of existing methods.

papers.title: Dirac-Interconnected Neural Elements: Discovering Modularity in Physical Systems Without Reduction

papers.abstract: We present an end-to-end QP-based policy framework that enables systematic policy construction with minimal domain-specific design, while preserving the transparency and interpretability of model-based control. The proposed policy representation supports both domain-randomized model-based auto-tuning, where policy parameters are optimized over distributions of disturbances and model variations, and black-box policy construction, where the problem is formulated in terms of a (possibly) unknown model without requiring explicit notions of states, inputs, or the underlying system dynamics. We establish connections to existing policy representations and control paradigms, including robust control, multilayer perceptrons, and robot learning, and interpret our end-to-end QP policies as a common abstraction of these approaches. We validate the resulting framework in both simulation and hardware, demonstrating a broad range of applications spanning robustness, automatic policy tuning, and control under unknown system dynamics.
bullets: Reduces domain-specific policy design through systematic QP-based construction.
Supports model-based auto-tuning over disturbances and model variations.
Also enables black-box policy construction without explicit states, inputs, or dynamics.
Connects robust control, multilayer perceptrons, and robot-learning policies under one abstraction.
Validated in simulation and hardware across robustness, automatic tuning, and unknown-dynamics control tasks.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Robust-control connections of the proposed QP policy on a double integrator regulation task. (a) Disturbance uncertainty: optimizing the outer objective approximates H2- and H∞-type feedback gains. (b) Model uncertainty: entropic risk interpolates between average- and worst-case performance. (c) Combined model and disturbance uncertainty: the learned QP policy is compared with nominal H∞ and worst case H∞ under plant uncertainty.

Fig. 4: Our end-to-end QP policy applied to a Crazyflie drone under a 5 m/s crosswind generated by an industrial fan with a flow-conditioning rack. Estimator, offset-compensation, and cost parameters are learned end to end, removing manual tuning and outperforming the hand-tuned baselines.

Fig. 5: Closed-loop position error under crosswind for the learned end-to-end QP policy and two manually tuned MPC baselines based on Bryson’s rule. Thick curves show the mean over five trials, thin transparent curves show individual trials, and light shading marks the trial range.
Fig. 2: Percentage of landings within a specified landing radius for 1000 vehicles, with and without domain randomization (DR). The inset highlights the upper landing-error tail.

Fig. 3: Closed-loop phase portraits of the learned projectionQP policy and the single-hidden-layer ReLU policy from the same five initial conditions near the hanging equilibrium. Both policies generate swing-up trajectories and converge to the upright equilibrium.

papers.selection_reason: End-to-end QP-based policies unify robust control and robot learning, fitting learned robotic control.
papers.title: End-to-end QP-based policies: A unified perspective on robust control and robot learning
papers.tldr: An end-to-end quadratic-programming policy framework unifies robust control and robot learning while retaining model-based interpretability and supporting known or unknown dynamics.

papers.abstract: Autonomous micro-mobility vehicles (MMVs) such as wheelchairs, scooters, and bicycles have the potential to improve mobility access and support safe low-speed transportation in pedestrian-shared spaces. Achieving MMV autonomy will require realistic, predictable MMV motion. However, many existing autonomous vehicle stacks rely on simplified kinematic models that fail to capture key MMV characteristics such as tire slip, friction, and wheel layouts, limiting realism and gradient-based optimization. In this paper, we explore differentiable formulations of dynamics models for autonomous micro-mobility systems. We first construct DiffKBM, a differentiable version of the kinematic bicycle model (KBM). Then, we introduce DiffGM3, a differentiable formulation of the General Micro-Mobility Model (GM3), a unified tire-based dynamics formulation for micro-mobility vehicles that supports a wide range of MMV configurations. DiffKBM and DiffGM3 enable end-to-end differentiable optimization through MMV dynamics, making them suitable for integration into differentiable autonomy stacks. We evaluate these dynamics models in both open-loop and closed-loop settings: (1) open-loop trajectory matching, where DiffKBM and DiffGM3 are integrated as a dynamics layer within DiffStack and optimized to reproduce real-world MMV trajectories, and (2) closed-loop autonomous navigation, where DiffKBM and DiffGM3 are paired with a differentiable MPC controller in CrowdNav pedestrian scenarios. In the open-loop setting, DiffGM3 outperforms DiffKBM in reproducing trajectories with improvements in ADE and NLL across bicycle, scooter, and motorcycle modes, and reductions in planning loss for bicycle and motorcycle trajectories. We also find that, in closed-loop settings, DiffGM3 improves on DiffKBM's CrowdNav performance by producing 55\% fewer collisions and a 75\% lower discomfort frequency for the bicycle mode.
bullets: Targets limitations of simplified vehicle models that omit tire slip, friction, and diverse wheel layouts.
Constructs DiffKBM, a differentiable kinematic bicycle model, and DiffGM3, a differentiable general micro-mobility dynamics model.
Evaluates both models in open-loop trajectory matching and closed-loop navigation with differentiable MPC in pedestrian scenarios.
DiffGM3 outperforms DiffKBM across bicycle, scooter, and motorcycle trajectory evaluations.
For bicycle navigation, DiffGM3 yields 55% fewer collisions and 75% lower discomfort frequency than DiffKBM.

figures.caption: Fig. 4: Overview of the DiffMPC pipeline integrated with DiffKBM or DiffGM3. At each timestep, the environment provides a state estimate xt , which is passed to the optimizer with the goal position and surrounding pedestrian states pedst . The optimizer proposes a control sequence u0:T−1 and uses either DiffKBM or DiffGM3 parameterized by learnable parameters ρKBM or ρGM3 to roll out predicted future states x0:T . A cost function is defined with learnable cost weights ρC. Because both the dynamics and the cost function are differentiable, gradients can be back-propagated through the prediction and cost modules to enable end-to-end learning of MMV dynamics parameters. The first control action u0 is applied to the environment, and the process repeats in a receding-horizon loop.

Fig. 2: DiffGM3 contains several differentiable components with sets of learnable parameters ρlean,ρtire, and ρVI. First, the steering control input δ is converted into tire-specific steering angles δi. This, along with the MMV’s previous longitudinal velocity vx, lateral velocity vy, and yaw rate r, is used to calculate tire velocities. Meanwhile, longitudinal and lateral accelerations, ax and ay, are used to transfer load among the tires, and the previous lean angle γ and roll rate γ̇ are used to determine the next lean angle. In addition to wheel angular velocity Ω, the results from these modules are inputs to the tire brush model, where forces and moments are computed. The outputs for each tire are integrated into the vehicle dynamics to obtain longitudinal, lateral, and yaw acceleration. Finally, the resulting position is calculated with Euler integration. This fully differentiable formulation allows gradients to backpropagate to each module so parameters can be tuned on MMV trajectory data.

Fig. 5: Closed-loop Navigation in Pedestrian Crowds Comparison between DiffGM3 Bicycle and DiffKBM: We show two unique scenarios each for DiffGM3 and DiffKBM. Longer pedestrian paths reflect the longer navigation time taken by the MMV to avoid moving pedestrians to reach its goal. Scenario 1: DiffGM3’s route reflects its ability to use real-world kinematics to avoid pedestrians when necessary, while DiffKBM’s simple kinematics forces it to attempt to fit right in between two pedestrians, resulting in a collision. Scenario 2: While both models reach the goal, DiffGM3’s longer route demonstrates less discomfort and higher minimum distance from pedestrians relative to DiffKBM’s direct route.

Fig. 3: Open-loop Trajectory Matching Comparison between the DiffKBM and DiffGM3: (a) On bicycle trajectories, DiffGM3 is able to stay on path because it has learnable parameters to prevent overturning. However, in some cases, it stops before the goal as shown by the red arrow, leading to a higher goal cost in the planning loss function. (b) On the other hand, the DiffKBM reaches its goal but veers off the ground-truth straight path, as indicated by the red arrow. This is due to the DiffKBM’s lack of support for realignment in its formula for yaw. (c) For a scooter, DiffGM3 is able to steer the scooter to its goal while avoiding other agents. (d) On the same trajectory, the DiffKBM causes the ego agent to turn towards another agent and slow down, preventing it from reaching its goal.

Fig. 1: DiffKBM implements wheelbase L as a learnable parameter in the steering component. The resulting turning rate θ̇ along with velocity are used in Euler integration to obtain the position. By making KBM end-to-end differentiable, we are able to tune L for an MMV with unknown wheelbase length.
TABLE I: Physical Parameters in the tire brush model.
TABLE II: Input Variables in the tire brush model.

TABLE V: Closed-loop Pedestrian Crowd Navigation Performance Comparison between DiffGM3 and DiffKBM: DiffGM3 prioritizes safety and demonstrates significantly fewer collisions across all vehicle configurations relative to DiffKBM. Specifically, in the baseline comparison between the two bicycle models, DiffGM3 produces 55% fewer collisions, with a 3% better success rate. DiffGM3’s incomplete rate and slower navigation time can be explained by its tendency to avoid collisions by veering away from the goal, resulting in situations where the vehicle is unable to arrive at the goal within the time limit. This also explains why DiffGM3’s discomfort frequency is 50%-75% better than DiffKBM’s across all modes. Moreover, DiffKBM’s faster navigation times are primarily the result of collisions ending the scenario early.

TABLE IV: Open-loop Trajectory Matching Evaluation Results: DiffGM3 outperforms DiffKBM in ADE (Bicycle: - 1.16%, Scooter -9.84%, Motorcycle: -2.37%) and NLL (Bicycle: -3.02%, Scooter -2.05%, Motorcycle: -4.75%) on all modes. For planning loss, DiffGM3 outperforms DiffKBM on bicycle (-4.16%) and motorcycle (-28.9%) trajectories, but performs worse on scooters (19.39%).

TABLE III: DiffGM3 parameters optimized using IMPTC trajectories. Align gain kalign and damping coefficients dyaw,droll help to stabilize the MMV and reduce oversteering. Moments of inertia Iz, Ix, and tire parameters are tuned because they are not easily measurable.

papers.selection_reason: Differentiable dynamics models for autonomous micro-mobility navigation and closed-loop planning fit robot navigation.
papers.title: Differentiable Dynamics for Autonomous Micro-Mobility Navigation
papers.tldr: The paper introduces differentiable micro-mobility dynamics models that improve trajectory matching and closed-loop navigation realism over a differentiable kinematic bicycle model.

papers.abstract: Uneven rotation and dropped frames make equal-angle assumptions unreliable for turntable reconstruction. We present OC-GS, an object-centric Gaussian splatting that refines each image's angle while maintaining a shared camera, rotation axis, and pivot. This orbit-consistent refinement jointly optimizes image-derived geometry and angles to reconstruct objects from sparse, irregular captures. On rendered objects with 12, 8, and 6 irregularly spaced views, OC-GS achieves mean foreground PSNR scores of 21.26, 19.36, and 15.83dB, respectively, exceeding all four evaluated pose-free Gaussian splatting baselines in each condition. Under a shared trainer, refining image-estimated angles improves mean foreground PSNR by 7.88dB over keeping those estimates fixed. An ablation study shows that both image-derived angle initialization and the shared motion model contribute to the improvement. On real captures, OC-GS's refinement increases mean foreground PSNR by 0.70dB. Results show that refining uncertain angles within a shared motion model improves reconstruction from sparse, irregular turntable captures.
bullets: Addresses uneven rotation and dropped frames that invalidate equal-angle assumptions.
Jointly optimizes image-derived angles and object geometry while sharing the camera, rotation axis, and pivot.
On rendered 12-, 8-, and 6-view captures, it achieves mean foreground PSNRs of 21.26, 19.36, and 15.83 dB, outperforming four evaluated pose-free baselines.
Angle refinement improves mean foreground PSNR by 7.88 dB over fixed image-estimated angles in a shared trainer; real captures improve by 0.70 dB.
Scope: evaluated on sparse, irregular turntable captures, with ablations confirming the value of angle initialization and the shared motion model.

figures.caption: Figure 1: OC-GS overview. (a) A fixed camera captures an object rotating about one axis with unequal angular gaps. (b) VGGT predicts initial geometry and cameras. A circle fit to the camera centers gives starting angles. OC-GS jointly refines the Gaussian scene, shared camera, axis, pivot, and per-view angles. (c) The shared turntable rig (blue) constrains the effective cameras, unlike independent cameras (orange). (d) Reconstruction is evaluated by comparing rendered and target images.

Figure 4: Selected examples of improvement with OC-GS. Black Flag (12 views), Therizinosaurus (8), and Hereford Bull (6) were selected to illustrate reconstruction gains. Each row uses the same target view and crop across methods. Scores report FG-PSNR (dB) / object-crop LPIPS. Bold indicates the best valid pose-free result.

Figure 2: Reconstruction quality under irregular capture. Mean target FG-PSNR with 12, 8, and 6 views (higher is better). Objects must have valid camera alignment in all five component configurations and all three seeds. Each baseline’s alignment failures are also excluded. Methods retain their own training settings.

Figure 3: Selected reconstructions under irregular capture. Hereford Bull with six views and Bathroom Set with twelve, shown at the first target view with the same crop across methods. SPFSplat has no valid placement for Hereford Bull.

Table 4: Pose initialization and camera models on real captures. Mean FG-PSNR (dB), evaluated using each reconstruction’s cameras. The named methods provide initial poses. The OC-GS rig keeps its azimuths fixed, while independent cameras are optimized from the predictions. Bold and underline indicate the best and second-best predictors within each block at the displayed precision.
Table 3: OC-GS with different initializers. We show the performance of different initializers and report them with the mean FG-PSNR (dB ↑). The best is bolded, which is from VGGT.

Table 1: Effect of the shared rig and angle refinement. FG-PSNR with the same trainer and VGGT predictions. Uniform angles assume equal spacing. Frozen angles retain image-derived estimates, while OC-GS refines them. The reference receives true angles. Means use the same valid objects per condition across all five variants and three seeds. Bold and underline indicate the best and second-best pose-free variants.

papers.abstract: We present ClearGS for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) from handheld videos with uneven viewpoint coverage and mixed frame quality. Rather than selecting frames with binary decisions, ClearGS uses Reliability-aware View Allocation (RVA) to assign graded raw-supervision weights based on appearance reliability, degradation risk, and geometric utility, while weakly reactivating useful suppressed frames to maintain trajectory coverage. Since weighting cannot restore details lost to blur or distortion, ClearGS further introduces Render-Guided In-Video Restoration (RIVR). The current 3DGS render provides a pose-aligned structural candidate, a frozen no-reference restoration expert restores the corresponding raw video observation without any clean reference image, and no-reference perceptual scores select among the render, restored observation, and high-frequency fused candidate. ClearGS then applies Full-Trajectory Repair Consolidation to revisit accepted repairs and preserve details introduced early. On GS2E and GSOTM, ClearGS achieves state-of-the-art overall performance, with consistent CLIP-IQA and MUSIQ gains and LPIPS reductions in most degradation settings, without paired sharp supervision or matched clean references.
bullets: Addresses mixed frame quality, uneven viewpoint coverage, blur, and distortion in handheld-video 3DGS.
Uses Reliability-aware View Allocation to assign graded supervision weights and weakly reactivate useful suppressed frames.
Introduces Render-Guided In-Video Restoration, selecting among rendered, restored, and fused candidates with no-reference perceptual scores.
Applies Full-Trajectory Repair Consolidation to revisit repairs and preserve details added early.
Reports state-of-the-art overall performance on GS2E and GSOTM, with consistent gains in CLIP-IQA and MUSIQ and lower LPIPS in most degradation settings.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of ClearGS. RVA assigns frame-wise raw-supervision weights from appearance reliability, degradation risk, and geometric utility, and weakly reactivates useful suppressed frames in uncovered trajectory regions. RIVR selects among the current render, restored raw observation, and detail-fused candidate using no-reference quality scores, then distills accepted pseudo observations with real observations.

Figure 1: Traditional pipelines either train or select handheld-video frames without graded reliability control, then repair degraded views using nearby references or cross-view cues that may share the same artifacts. ClearGS instead uses RVA to separate appearance reliability from geometric utility, and applies no-reference RIVR to add selected repair evidence without matched clean references.

Figure 5: Qualitative comparison on five GS2E scenes. From left to right: the input 3DGS, DiFiX3D, GeoQuery, SyncFix, ClearGS, and the ground truth. ClearGS recovers sharper object boundaries and local details while preserving the scene appearance.

Figure 3: Qualitative comparison of renderings at observed input camera poses produced by all-view 3DGS and the Select-view initialization of ClearGS. Red boxes highlight regions where our reconstruction better preserves thin structures, object boundaries, and local appearance relative to all-view supervision.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison of repair outputs on two GS2E scenes. Each row shows the same camera pose. From left to right, the panels show the common pre-repair 3DGS rendering, the repairs produced by DiFiX3D and GeoQuery, and the repair selected by ClearGS.

Table 5: Ablation of RIVR candidate selection. “w/o Obs.” replaces the raw video observation Ot with the current render Rt as the input to Restormer, while “w/o Ft” removes the high-frequency fused candidate. The remaining repairdistillation pipeline is unchanged.

Table 1: RVA notation, parameter settings, and supervision policy. The standard supervision conditions are evaluated from top to bottom. Afterward, trajectory coverage compensation may reactivate a suppressed frame in an uncovered trajectory bin with a fixed weak-supervision weight.

Table 3: Perceptual comparison on GS2E and GSOTM at observed input poses. GS2E averages ten scenes per blur level, and GSOTM averages four scenes per degradation type. LPIPS uses sharp targets; CLIP-IQA and MUSIQ are no-reference metrics. Best and second-best results are highlighted.

papers.abstract: Medical vision-language model (VLM) post-training is commonly evaluated through answer accuracy. We examine how changes in accuracy and training objectives relate to image-conditioned decisions in a controlled Qwen2.5-VL-3B study on PMC-VQA. We compare supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) restricted to the language model, expanded multimodal adaptation scopes, standard answer-only Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), and a counterfactual evidence objective. On 2,000 clean-test questions, language model LoRA SFT changes correct-image accuracy by +1.10 percentage points (95% paired bootstrap CI:-0.85 to +3.05), while visual-benefit events decrease by 2.40 points and image sensitivity decreases by 5.60 points. Paired records reveal 155 acquired and 203 lost visual-benefit events. Broader adaptation yields lower correct-image accuracy than language-model LoRA SFT. Standard GRPO produces mixed-reward groups and parameter updates, with an uncertain clean test accuracy change. A generation audit reveals that canonical option scores can follow a different token path from generated answers. With scores taken along the greedy generation path, the evidence target improves on the training set; its gains over standard GRPO remain inconsistent on validation data at matched training doses. Sample-level analyses trace how evidence scores, decision margins, and generated answers change during post-training. This empirical and measurement audit identifies gaps between optimization activity, target acquisition, and useful held-out visual behavior.
bullets: Evaluates SFT, LoRA, broader multimodal adaptation, standard GRPO, and a counterfactual evidence objective in Qwen2.5-VL-3B on PMC-VQA.
Language-model LoRA SFT slightly increases correct-image accuracy, but decreases visual-benefit events and image sensitivity on clean-test questions.
Broader adaptation performs worse on correct-image accuracy than language-model LoRA SFT; standard GRPO yields mixed rewards and uncertain test changes.
Evidence-target gains appear on training data but remain inconsistent on validation data at matched training doses.
Generation audits show that canonical option scores may not reflect the token path used for generated answers, complicating measurement.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Adaptation-scope comparison using VALID-selected checkpoints on a common clean-test cohort. The three configurations vary which components are trained: language attention adapters, the multimodal merger, and vision adapters. Their effects reflect the combined changes in trainable capacity, optimization, and regularization.

Figure 6: Standard GRPO training diagnostics and clean-test performance. The training signal is the fraction of prompt groups with nonzero reward variance. A separate checkpoint audit verifies adapter updates. The clean-test comparison shows a small accuracy change with a paired confidence interval spanning zero.

Figure 2: SFT performance under the frozen clean-test protocol. Paired-bootstrap intervals show decreases in VBR and IS and an increase in pattern111, while the task and C-S changes remain uncertain. NoImage accuracy is nearly unchanged.

Figure 3: Paired pattern transitions and bidirectional event flows from M0 to M1-L. Matrix entries are QA counts and sum to 2,000; color uses log(1 + count). The 155 VBR gains and 203 losses recover the aggregate -2.40-point change.

Figure 7: Generation-path measurement and decision margins. Panels A-B show the natural token branch and trace-consistency checks. Panels C-D compare M4-500 with M2-500 on two VALID examples: evidence and decision margins can move in different directions or share a change in the correct-image gold score. The evidence-up/decision-down example is drawn from three cases meeting both strict criteria.

Figure 4: Examples from three paired-transition categories. Labels follow the dataset annotations. The first two questions share a source image but concern different panels and use different replacement images. The third shows a gain in correct-image-only success.

Figure 8: Training-target acquisition and held-out transfer at matched doses. Panel A reports TRAIN score gains relative to M1-L. Panels B-D compare M4 with standard GRPO at equal prompt counts. The diagnostic cohorts contain 256 TRAIN pattern100 questions, 188 VALID pattern100 questions, and 112 VALID pattern110 questions; behavioral comparisons use the diagnostic VALID cohort of 645. Score effects are in raw branch-logit units and behavioral effects are in percentage points.

Figure 1: Evaluation under Correct, NoImage, and Shuffled image conditions. The three-bit patterns record answer correctness in C/N/S order. Visual-benefit and visual-harm events decompose the Correct-minus-Shuffled accuracy difference; the full patterns also describe success under the NoImage condition.

papers.selection_reason: Controlled audit of medical VLM post-training objectives and visual utility, directly relevant to multimodal LLM training behavior.
papers.title: From Reward Signal to Visual Utility: A Controlled Audit of Medical VLM Post-Training
papers.tldr: A controlled audit finds that medical VLM post-training can improve answer accuracy without improving—and sometimes reducing—the model’s useful reliance on visual evidence.
